analysis.one_liner: Reinstates expired Superfund taxes on polluting industries to pay for toxic site cleanups.
analysis.headline: The Polluter Pays Restoration Act, which would have put chemical and oil companies back on the hook for Superfund cleanup funding, never got a vote: it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on March 25, 2010 and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Superfund program cleans up the nation's worst abandoned toxic waste sites. Until 1995, the program was funded mainly by taxes on the chemical and oil companies whose products create hazardous waste. Those taxes expired, and since then general taxpayer money has covered the cleanups. This bill would have reinstated those taxes through 2016, shifting cleanup costs from ordinary taxpayers back onto industry. The bill was introduced by Sen. Frank Lautenberg and six colleagues, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who would no longer foot the bill for cleaning up toxic waste sites created by chemical and petroleum products, and communities living near Superfund sites that would get a more reliably funded cleanup program.
analysis.who_benefits_short: General taxpayers and communities near toxic sites

how_it_helps.text: The bill reinstates the Hazardous Substance Superfund financing rate, an excise tax on crude oil and hazardous chemicals, from enactment through January 1, 2017.
It also reinstates the corporate environmental income tax for the same period, so polluting industries rather than general taxpayers finance Superfund cleanups.
The bill's title and design are explicitly built on the 'polluter pays' principle that existed before the taxes lapsed in 1995.

analysis.who_pays: Chemical manufacturers, crude oil producers and refiners, and other large corporations, which would pay the reinstated excise and income taxes; some of those costs could be passed through to consumers in the prices of fuel and chemical products.

drawbacks.text: The reinstated excise taxes on crude oil and chemicals would raise production costs that companies could pass along to consumers in the form of higher prices for fuel and chemical-based goods.

The corporate environmental income tax applies to corporations generally based on their income, not strictly to the amount of hazardous waste a particular company creates, so some companies would pay without generating Superfund liabilities.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill shifts a public cleanup burden from general taxpayers onto the industries whose products create hazardous waste, which is the core of a strong benefit. The costs are real but narrow: modestly higher prices for fuel and chemical products, and a corporate tax that is not perfectly matched to each company's pollution. On balance, the benefits to taxpayers and communities near toxic sites outweigh the costs, though the bill's simple revival of old taxes is a blunt instrument.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died there when the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Sen. Frank Lautenberg introduced the Polluter Pays Restoration Act on March 25, 2010, joined by co-sponsors including Sens. Menendez, Whitehouse, Sanders, Merkley, and Cardin.
The bill had seven cosponsors: six Senate Democrats and the Senate's one independent, Bernie Sanders; no Republicans signed on.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance on the day it was introduced.
That referral was the bill's last recorded action; the Finance Committee held no markup and the full Senate never voted on it before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.
This was not the first attempt: Congress let the original Superfund taxes lapse at the end of 1995, which is what the bill sought to undo, and the taxes have remained expired since.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Chemical, petroleum, and other large corporations came out ahead: they avoided the reinstated cleanup taxes and continued to leave Superfund funding to general taxpayer revenue.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Chemical, oil, and other large corporations

sides.party_line_note: All seven cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's lone independent; no Republican cosponsored, and the Democratic-led Finance Committee took no action.

industries.note: The bill reinstates the Superfund excise tax on hazardous chemicals, directly charging the industry whose products generate much of the toxic waste the program cleans up. Blocking the bill keeps those cleanup costs on general taxpayers.
The reinstated Hazardous Substance Superfund financing rate is levied on crude oil, including the bill's technical fix to also cover imported crude. Industry avoided the tax by the bill's failure.

The corporate environmental income tax applies to large corporations based on income, so many firms beyond the chemical and oil sectors would have paid. Its expiration kept that money with corporate balance sheets.
A more reliably funded Superfund would mean more cleanup work, though the bill funds the program through taxes rather than new appropriations. Its effects on this industry are indirect.
